summary: Defines the CMS encrypted key package content type, used to encrypt content that holds a key package such as a symmetric or asymmetric key package. It is independent of transport.

eli5.summary: A bundle of keys can be sealed in a locked box for travel. This describes that locked box.

subtitle: A CMS wrapper that lets encrypted key packages carry their own authorization check.

tldr.problem: CMS Content Constraints can authorize who may produce a plaintext key package, but not who may produce an encrypted one, because the encryption layers cannot be constrained. Intermediate systems that cannot decrypt a key package still may need to check its producer.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6032 defines an encrypted key package content type with its own object identifier. It is a choice of EncryptedData, EnvelopedData or AuthEnvelopedData, so that identifier can be listed in a signer's certificate.
tldr.outcome: A producer can be authorized for encrypted key packages, and the recipient can check the outer signer first and the inner signer after decrypting. RFC 6032 also adds an attribute that names the key needed to decrypt EncryptedData.

today: RFC 6032 is a Proposed Standard, published in December 2010. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What the Encrypted Key Package Is
sections.content:
The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) can sign, digest, authenticate or encrypt arbitrary content, and CMS messages can have many layers. RFC 6031 and RFC 5958 define symmetric key package and asymmetric key package content types that CMS can sign or encrypt.

RFC 6032 defines the encrypted key package content type. It encrypts a content that includes a key package, and it is transport independent. CMS can then sign, digest, authenticate or further encrypt it.
sections.eli5: Keys can be put in a locked box, and this document describes the box. It does not say how the box is mailed.

sections.title: Why Plain CMS Layers Were Not Enough
sections.content:
The CMS Content Constraints (CCC) certificate extension from RFC 6010 lets a recipient decide whether the originator of an authenticated content type is authorized to produce it. CCC cannot constrain the structures that provide layers of protection, such as SignedData, EnvelopedData, EncryptedData, DigestData, CompressedData, AuthenticatedData, ContentCollection, ContentWithAttributes or AuthEnvelopedData.

That works for plaintext key packages, because the producer's certificate can list the content type. It does not work for encrypted key material. In some key management systems, encrypted key packages are passed between entities that cannot decrypt them, and checking the producer's authorization at those intermediate points may still be wanted.

The fix is a distinct content type. Its object identifier is put in the originator's CCC certificate extension, and the originator wraps the encrypted key package in a SignedData, EnvelopedData or AuthEnvelopedData so the recipient can check authorization during certification path validation.
sections.eli5: A normal locked box has no label saying what is inside, so nobody can check if the sender may send keys. A labelled box fixes that.

sections.title: The EncryptedKeyPackage Structure
sections.content:
EncryptedKeyPackage is an ASN.1 CHOICE of three existing CMS protecting types. The RFC says it differs from them only in the object identifier and one tag.

  • encrypted is an EncryptedData, for simple symmetric encryption where sender and receiver already share the key. An unprotected attribute can carry a key identifier.
  • enveloped is a EnvelopedData tagged [0], where transferred key management information lets the receiver decrypt. The details depend on the key management algorithm used.
  • authEnveloped is an AuthEnvelopedData tagged [1], for authenticated encryption. It carries a message authentication code that covers the content and the authenticated attributes.

The content type is identified by id-ct-KP-encryptedKeyPkg, an object identifier under the key-package-content-types arc with final value 2.
sections.eli5: The box comes in three styles: one for people who already share a key, one that carries the key information inside, and one that also has a tamper seal.

sections.title: What Implementations Must Support
sections.content:
Implementations MUST support the EnvelopedData choice, SHOULD support the EncryptedData choice, and MAY support AuthEnvelopedData.

For EnvelopedData and EncryptedData, implementations MUST support an EncryptedKeyPackage that holds a SignedData wrapping either a SymmetricKeyPackage or an AsymmetricKeyPackage. For AuthEnvelopedData, they MUST support an EncryptedKeyPackage that holds a bare SymmetricKeyPackage or AsymmetricKeyPackage, and supporting the signed forms is OPTIONAL. Implementations that decrypt the content MUST support the signed forms. An EncryptedKeyPackage MUST contain at least one SymmetricKeyPackage or AsymmetricKeyPackage, and implementations MAY support additional encapsulating layers.

If the originator and recipient support different innermost content, the RFC says this is not a concern because originators should know the recipient's capabilities. How those capabilities are exchanged is out of scope.
sections.eli5: Everyone must know how to open the most common box. The fancier boxes are optional extras.

sections.title: Checking Both Signers
sections.content:
Authorization is checked layer by layer. The RFC's example is a SignedData that holds an encrypted key package, which holds another SignedData, which holds a symmetric key package. A recipient that can decrypt performs these steps before accepting the key material:

  1. Verify the signature on the outer SignedData.
  2. Build and validate a certification path for the outer signer and confirm that signer may produce the encrypted key package.
  3. Decrypt the encrypted key package.
  4. Verify the signature on the inner SignedData.
  5. Build and validate a path for the inner signer and confirm it may produce the symmetric key package. The validator may reuse attributes and public keys from the second step as inputs.
  6. Use the symmetric key material.

In RFC 6010 terms the encrypted key package is a leaf node, so more authorization checks may be needed after decryption. The inner authorization check need not use an intermediate SignedData layer. With AuthEnvelopedData, the second check would begin at the authEnveloped field.
sections.eli5: First you check the stamp on the outside of the box. Then you open it and check the stamp on the note inside before using the keys.

sections.title: The Content Decryption Key Identifier
sections.content:
The RFC also defines an unprotected attribute, content-decryption-key-identifier, for use with EncryptedData. It names the symmetric key needed to decrypt the content when there is any ambiguity.

Its value is an OCTET STRING, and the syntax imposes no structure on it. There MUST be only one instance of the attribute and only one value in it. Because there can be several layers of encryption, the attribute may appear in more than one place in the overall key package. Each occurrence is evaluated independently and identifies the key for its own layer.
sections.eli5: It is a name tag on the box that says which key opens it, which helps when you own many keys.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Implementers are strongly encouraged to follow generally accepted principles of secure key management. The security considerations of RFC 5083, RFC 5652, RFC 5911, RFC 5912, RFC 5958 and RFC 6031 apply, and so do those of RFC 6010 when CCC is used for authorization.

The encrypted key package might not prove who sent it if the content encryption algorithm does not support authenticated key exchange. Proof of origin needs another security protocol, which is why wrapping the key package in a SignedData is required for the EnvelopedData and EncryptedData choices. Finally, the CMS SignedData validation rules MUST be used, and the PKCS #7 validation rules MUST NOT be used.
sections.eli5: A locked box alone does not prove who sent it, so the sender should also sign it. Be careful with keys in general.

sections.title: Object Identifiers and the ASN.1 Module
sections.content:
The document uses object identifiers for a CMS content type, a CMS attribute and the ASN.1 module, all given in Appendix A. All of them are registered in an arc delegated by RSADSI to the SMIME Working Group.

Appendix A holds the normative ASN.1 module, EncryptedKeyPackageModuleV1, which imports its building blocks from the RFC 5911 and RFC 5912 modules.
sections.eli5: Each new kind of box and name tag gets its own official serial number so nobody mixes them up.
